{"id": "41:34/q02", "question": "What is the function of the second lā in the contrast?", "turns_on": "Whether lā is syntactically added for emphasis, supplies a reciprocal negation, or distinguishes instances within each generic noun; Samin disputes an objection that conflates the last with the first.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q02/p1", "position": "It is an extra particle reinforcing the denial that good and evil are equal.", "reasons": "Akhfash compares 57:29 and 75:1; Tabari reports Basran grammarians and cites 75:2 while recording an objection about 75:1; Zajjaj, al-Farra, and later commentators adopt or report emphasis. Samin notes that istawā needs two complements and compares 35:21 and 40:58. Alusi compares 35:21; Samarrai notes 35:19–22 and adds differences within each class. Burhan reports the explanation that istawa requires two arguments and records a reading on which the second la is extra."}, {"id": "41:34/q02/p2", "position": "It meaningfully negates the reciprocal comparison: neither good equals evil nor evil equals good.", "reasons": "Akhfash illustrates with Abdullah and Zayd; Tabari says each side is unequal to the other; Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur understand an ellipsis in both directions. Jishumi reports this as an alternative to emphasis. Burhan also reports the alternative that repeating la expressly denies equality in both directions."}, {"id": "41:34/q02/p3", "position": "It meaningfully denies equality within the classes of good deeds and evil deeds, whose instances vary in degree.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari is reported by Samin; Bursevi cites al-Kashshaf and ranges from removing harm to greater good and from minor to major sin; Alusi says this yields answering the worse with the best; Elmalılı and Samarrai also see internal variation. Samin rejects the objection that this analysis still treats lā as extra. Burhan prefers this contextual reading and says the waw joins clauses while the second la retains its force."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q03", "question": "Why use the abstract nouns for good and evil?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q03/p1", "position": "The nouns portray goodness and evil at their full extent and lead into ethical counsel.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur contrasts the abstract nouns with nouns naming the doers."}, {"id": "41:34/q03/p2", "position": "The basic nouns for good and evil negate equality more strongly than the corresponding feminine superlatives would.", "reasons": "Samarrai contrasts hasanah and sayyi'ah with husna, the feminine superlative of ahsan, and su'a; he says husna would suggest possible equality, whereas the verse's wording negates even a lesser difference, and he mentions 39:10."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q04", "question": "How does the opening contrast connect to the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Whether 41:34 is attached chiefly to 41:33's praise or reaches back to the opponents' obstruction in 41:26; Ibn Ashur records both connections.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q04/p1", "position": "It continues the praise of the caller to God in 41:33 by contrasting the believer's good state and the disbeliever's evil.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares 40:58; Tabrisi contrasts the opponents' disruption in 41:26 with Muhammad's call in 41:33, saying his practice confirms his message. Ibn Ashur also sees 41:30's divine promise exposing the gulf from the deniers."}, {"id": "41:34/q04/p2", "position": "It resumes the disbelievers' obstruction of Quran recitation and consoles the Prophet, preparing his gentle response.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur points to 41:26 and 41:5; Asad identifies scurrilous objections and hostile criticism and compares 13:22; Kuranyolu's Razi cites the closed hearts and noise during recitation."}, {"id": "41:34/q04/p3", "position": "It gives the practical response to hostility that may confront a caller to God.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says to convey good gently and tactfully; Tabatabai says it follows the praise of inviting to God and teaches the best way to make an impact. {"id": "41:34/q05", "question": "What should one do when told to repel with what is best?", "turns_on": "Whether the command is read as a broad practice or a particular form of response; the greeting reports are treated by Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan as a beginning of the broader practice.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q05/p1", "position": "Answer injury, insult, anger, and ignorance with patience, forbearance, pardon, and kindness.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives patience when angry, forbearance toward ignorance, pardon when wronged; Tabari compares 23:96. Razi says repeated restraint shames offenders; Umar says answer another's disobedience to God with one's own obedience. Abu Firas's poem praises continual pardon. Qurtubi transmits Ali's advice to Qanbar and two poems on silence frustrating a fool, plus Mahmud al-Warraq's advice by relative standing. Bursevi cites the Prophet's practice of ties, pardon, and good treatment; Ibn Ashur notes his Quranic character and Torah description. Study Quran compares 23:96 and 29:46 and cites hadith on ties, giving, pardon, and no reciprocal harm. Nahhas states the broad instruction as responding in the best manner or condition."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p2", "position": "Greet the opponent with peace upon meeting.", "reasons": "Mujahid and Ata are repeatedly named. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say greeting starts the wider virtue but does not exhaust it; Ata also speaks of answering harm with peace."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p3", "position": "Meet falsehood or error with truth.", "reasons": "Tabrisi includes this with forbearance and pardon; Tabatabai does likewise; Study Quran attributes it to Ṭs."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p4", "position": "Return a good deed, praise, or material generosity to the offender, beyond mere forgiveness.", "reasons": "Nasafi contrasts praise with insult and a good act with a bad act; Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalılı, and Kuranyolu's Zamakhshari distinguish benevolence from pardon. Bursevi's Greatest Imam anecdote says praise induced an abuser to praise him. Ibn Atiyya includes generosity in paying and collecting debts."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p5", "position": "Turn away from the offender's harm or refrain from replying.", "reasons": "Mujahid recommends turning away; Ali, as quoted by Qurtubi, recommends silence to Qanbar, and Qurtubi adduces poems that silence most frustrates an insulting fool."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p6", "position": "Shake hands affectionately and sincerely when meeting.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi applies the verse this way, citing a report that handshaking removes rancor; al-Bara's Prophetic report says two Muslims clasping hands have sins fall away."}, {"id": "41:34/q05/p7", "position": "Repel one's own impulses toward vice by practicing virtue.", "reasons": "Study Quran explicitly gives this inward application; Biqai includes harm from oneself as well as from others; Qashani contrasts the heart with the lower self and warns that evil for evil grows."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q06", "question": "What object is omitted after 'repel'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q06/p1", "position": "The omitted object is evil, supplied by the preceding contrast.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares 13:22 and 23:96; Study Quran notes the absence of an expressed object before listing anger, error, ignorance, and wrongdoing as possible instances."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q07", "question": "What does 'that which is best' add to the command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q07/p1", "position": "It urges the finest available good response, greater than simple pardon, and intensifies the command.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, and Alusi say the implied question and answer stress the matter; one who can do the best can readily do a lesser good. Nasafi compares two good responses. Ibn Ashur says anger makes retaliation natural, so the superlative encourages virtue; Study Quran notes 'better' can mean more beautiful or virtuous. Alusi says the comparator is general and omitted. Nahhas glosses the best response as the best manner or condition of responding."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q08", "question": "What are the scope and limits of the command to respond well?", "turns_on": "The extent to which personal pardon remains best when God's limits or greater harms are at stake, and whether the Prophet's handshaking of Jafar establishes a general practice.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q08/p1", "position": "It directs the Prophet and community toward patience and pardon during personal injury and preaching, while preserving God's limits and avoiding greater harm.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the Prophet completed moral excellence and cites Aisha: he did not avenge himself except for God's inviolable limits; the community is encouraged and 42:40 promises reward. Study Quran says do not surrender to an enemy or accept falsehood, and avoid returning harm if that will not cause greater harm; it cites 13:27, 23:96, 28:54. Islahi says proportionate retaliation remains permitted under 16:125–126, but forgiveness better serves preaching and reform."}, {"id": "41:34/q08/p2", "position": "Patience is appropriate while truth is being conveyed; after active destructive rejection, taking opponents to task can be better or necessary.", "reasons": "Islahi says the Meccan opponents urged to forgive were later punished by the Companions at God's direction after conclusive communication of truth. Ibn Ashur says greater excellence may require foregoing a particular act of clemency."}, {"id": "41:34/q08/p3", "position": "Handshaking is an applicable social practice.

", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi cites the saying that it removes rancor; Sufyan argues the Prophet's greeting of Jafar applies to the community, opposing Malik's restriction."}, {"id": "41:34/q08/p4", "position": "The Prophet's greeting of Jafar was special, so handshaking should not be generalized from it.", "reasons": "Qurtubi transmits Malik's opposition and Sufyan's contrary reasoning in the same note."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q09", "question": "Was the command to respond well abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether later fighting supersedes this imperative or the best response varies with the situation, while pardon remains morally commended.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q09/p1", "position": "The sword or fighting verse abrogated the instruction, although forbearance and good company remain recommended.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports exegetes citing 9:5; Qurtubi holds abrogation but preserves overlooking, forbearance, and good company as recommended."}, {"id": "41:34/q09/p2", "position": "The instruction remains a conditional moral norm alongside permissible or necessary retaliation.", "reasons": "Islahi cites 16:125–126 for lawful proportional retaliation and better patience, then distinguishes the stage of conveying truth from active attacks. {"id": "41:34/q10", "question": "What result can the better response have on an enemy?", "turns_on": "How literally ka-annahu presents friendship: an actual change, an outward resemblance with uncertain sincerity, or a usual partial result that can deepen.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q10/p1", "position": "The enemy can become a close, affectionate ally or friend through kindness.", "reasons": "Muqatil says restraint and pardon can transform opposition; Tabari, Baghawi, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Bursevi, Tabatabai, and others affirm the social change. Qashani adds remorse and expulsion of Satan; Biqai pictures practical aid and compares hot water cleansing dirt. Jurjani adduces the Prophetic saying that hearts love their benefactors and cites this verse as a Quranic parallel. Islahi grounds the change in human responsiveness to persistent goodwill; Muhammad won sincere companions, though hardened hearts remained unmoved."}, {"id": "41:34/q10/p2", "position": "The enemy ordinarily only appears like an intimate friend in outward behavior; true intimacy may remain absent.", "reasons": "Qushayri denies full sincerity; Ibn Atiyya explains the simile ka-annahu; Abu Hayyan and Alusi report him. Ibn Ashur says affection enters and hostility recedes but ordinarily falls short of full friendship. Alusi qualifies that this is only a usual minimum: hostility can sometimes disappear altogether, citing a poem."}, {"id": "41:34/q10/p3", "position": "It quickly yields visible kindness and may win religious opponents into affectionate solidarity.", "reasons": "Tabrisi describes an enemy in religion resembling an ally in faith and kinship. Ibn Ashur treats the sudden-result clause as the command's practical benefit; Qashani lists quieted hostility, remorse, guidance, and becoming close."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q11", "question": "What do walī and ḥamīm mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q11/p1", "position": "Walī is an ally or supporter, and ḥamīm is a close relative or intimate friend.", "reasons": "Qatada says close ally or relative; Ikrima separates friend from near relative. Ibn Atiyya adds care and protection; Ibn Ashur says the two qualities jointly oppose enmity. Damghani gives close relative or intimate friend for ḥamīm. Abu Zayd calls close relative the Arab usage of hamim; Muhammad b. Yazid supports the sense intimate associate by citing the Arab distinction between intimates and the public. Majaz gives both close relative and intimate; Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha gives close blood relative."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q12", "question": "How does the sudden-result clause work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether ka-annahu walī functions as a circumstantial clause or the predicate of the relative subject, and how idhā is governed.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q12/p1", "position": "The relative phrase is subject, sudden idhā is predicate, and ka-annahu walī is circumstantial.", "reasons": "Samin presents this analysis as making the enemy present in the state of an intimate friend."}, {"id": "41:34/q12/p2", "position": "The relative phrase is subject and ka-annahu walī is its predicate; idhā attaches to resemblance or has no governor.", "reasons": "Samin reports the two subanalyses of sudden idhā."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q13", "question": "What does the sudden idhā convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q13/p1", "position": "It conveys the rapid appearance of kindness's effect on an enemy.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur identifies the prefixed particle as suddenative and ties its force to the command's promised benefit."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q14", "question": "Why describe the enemy as 'the one between you and whom there is enmity'?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression's force lies in general eloquence or in its open range of hostilities; the readings can coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q14/p1", "position": "The fuller relative expression is more eloquent than simply saying 'your enemy'.", "reasons": "Alusi calls it more expressive despite its length; Tabatabai reports a view that also calls it concise."}, {"id": "41:34/q14/p2", "position": "The expression leaves enmity indefinite in kind, strength, and duration, implying stronger kindness for entrenched hostility.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur draws this range from the relative construction."}]}
{"id": "41:34/q15", "question": "What occasion or person is said to underlie the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's transformation fits Abu Sufyan's biography, especially whether his later closeness came from kindness or conversion; Abu Jahl is a separate reported addressee.", "positions": [{"id": "41:34/q15/p1", "position": "It concerned Abu Sufyan, whose hostility softened through the Prophet's marriage tie with Umm Habiba and later Islam.", "reasons": "Muqatil or Muqatil ibn Hayyan is transmitted; Jishumi names Ramlah, Umm Habiba; Baghawi and Bursevi add Islam and kinship; Alusi calls him later close to Sunnis and remarks on his grandson Yazid. Qurtubi prefers this report because the verse depicts a former enemy becoming intimate; Elmalılı cites him as an example."}, {"id": "41:34/q15/p2", "position": "It concerned Abu Jahl's harm to Muhammad, for which the Prophet was told to show patience and pardon.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives Abu Jahl and adds seeking refuge from Satan; Mawardi and Qurtubi transmit this account. {"id": "41:35/q01", "question": "What does yulaqqaha mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb emphasizes reception of a granted quality or the person's effort to cultivate it.", "positions": [{"id": "41:35/q01/p1", "position": "To receive or be granted the virtue, and thus accept and practice it.", "reasons": "Jishumi explains talaqqi as receiving a report from another person and cites al-Mu'arrij's gloss 'accepting.' {"id": "41:35/q03", "question": "How is yulaqqaha read?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is the passive of talqiya or derives from mulaqat, meeting.", "positions": [{"id": "41:35/q03/p1", "position": "The common passive reading means that the trait is received or granted.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes this to the majority; al-Samin calls it the passive of talqiya."}, {"id": "41:35/q03/p2", "position": "Talha ibn Musarrif and Ibn Kathir in one transmission read yulaqaha, meaning to meet or encounter it.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan gives the meaning and names both readers; al-Samin derives it from mulaqat; al-Alusi reports the same variant."}]}

{"id": "51:11/q03", "question": "What is the immersion (ghamrah) that envelops them?", "turns_on": "Which enveloping state is stressed: epistemic error, heedlessness itself, sinful conduct, or desire and conjecture.", "positions": [{"id": "51:11/q03/p1", "position": "An overwhelming covering of ignorance, falsehood, misguidance, blindness, doubt, or confusion.", "reasons": "Nahhas explains the covering of falsehood and ignorance by a person or water covering one who enters. {"id": "51:11/q05", "question": "What does 'heedless' mean, and of what are they heedless?", "turns_on": "The scope and object of sahw: general inattention, divine duties, the hereafter, conveyed truth, prayer specifically, or perfection.", "positions": [{"id": "51:11/q05/p1", "position": "Inattentive, distracted, or forgetful, with the heart losing track of what matters.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports al-Layth's Arabic definition of sahw as inattention and the heart losing track. {"id": "51:52/q01", "question": "What does “likewise” compare?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative recalls the preceding rejection or anticipates the following statement.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q01/p1", "position": "The present rejection of Muhammad repeats earlier peoples’ rejection of their messengers and their sorcery or madness charges.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq call it the same recurring state; al-Bayḍāwī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī say the following clause explains the comparison. {"id": "51:52/q02", "question": "How is “likewise” construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "The case of the kāf and whether a verb after negative ما can govern it.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q02/p1", "position": "It is nominative, the predicate of an omitted subject: “the matter is so.”", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās states this option; al-Qurṭubī links it to a warning to associators; al-Samīn calls it stronger; al-Ālūsī says it points forward."}, {"id": "51:52/q02/p2", "position": "It is accusative, qualifying an omitted verbal noun or expressing a comparison with earlier messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās relates it to Quraysh’s predecessors; al-Qurṭubī applies that reading to disobedient monotheists. {"id": "51:52/q03", "question": "Who are “those before them” and “them”?", "turns_on": "Whether earlier communities as a whole or their unbelievers alone are meant.", "positions": [{"id": "51:52/q03/p1", "position": "They are earlier communities before Quraysh or the Meccan unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly calls them Quraysh’s predecessors.
